stages.title: State provision: pros and cons
stages.sub: Weigh up the real advantages and disadvantages of the state providing a good instead of the market.

steps.q: A vaccine protects other people too, not just the person who takes it. If a private firm prices the vaccine only on what the buyer gains, does it count the protection given to everyone else?
steps.right: No, it leaves that benefit out
steps.wrong: Yes, it charges for all of it
steps.hint: Think about who the firm can actually charge money to.

steps.q: If the state instead provides the vaccine free, does it need to ignore the protection given to other people when deciding how many to supply?
steps.right: No, it can supply based on the full benefit to society
steps.wrong: Yes, it must still ignore that benefit
steps.hint: The state is not trying to make a profit from each individual buyer.

steps.q: Laying two separate sets of water pipes into every street, one for each of two rival water companies, would mean digging up the road twice. Would having a single provider avoid this?
steps.right: Yes, one network avoids the second dig
steps.wrong: No, two networks would still cost the same
steps.hint: Think about how much extra digging a second, competing network would need.

steps.q: If the state runs the water network as the single provider, does it need to build a second, rival network as well?
steps.wrong: Yes, competition still requires a second one
steps.hint: What was the point of there being only one network in the first place?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: The state pays for free hospital care using money collected from taxpayers. Where does that money come from?
steps.right: Taxes taken from people's income and spending
steps.wrong: Fees charged to patients when they are treated
steps.hint: The care is free to the patient, so who is actually paying for it?

steps.q: That tax money could instead have been left with taxpayers to spend on other things, or used to fund schools instead. What do we call the best alternative given up by spending it on hospitals?
steps.right: The opportunity cost of that spending
steps.hint: You already know the term for the best thing given up when money is spent one way rather than another.

steps.q: A GP surgery lets patients see a doctor without paying anything at the point of use. Does the patient hand over money for that appointment?
steps.right: No, the appointment costs the patient nothing directly
steps.wrong: Yes, they pay a fee at the surgery
steps.hint: Think about what the patient hands over at the reception desk.

steps.q: If more people want appointments than there are slots available, and price cannot be used to sort this out, how do patients end up getting seen?
steps.right: They queue or wait for a slot
steps.wrong: The price rises until fewer people want one
steps.hint: Price cannot ration it here, since it is free. What else sorts out who gets served first?
